exercises.title: Batch vs Streaming Trade-offs
exercises.subtitle: Learn the IT-English vocabulary comparing batch and streaming data processing: latency, throughput, windowing and exactly-once.

questions.q: What characterises 'batch processing'?
options: Processing each event instantly
Processing large groups of data on a schedule rather than as it arrives
No data storage
Real-time only
questions.explanation: Batch jobs process accumulated data periodically; streaming processes events continuously as they arrive.

questions.q: Streaming is chosen when low 'latency' matters. What is latency here?
options: The total data size
The delay between an event occurring and being processed
The number of servers
The schema version
questions.explanation: Latency is the time from event to result; streaming minimises it for near-real-time needs.

questions.q: A streaming job uses 'windowing'. What does that do?
options: Opens a UI window
Groups events into time-based buckets for aggregation
Deletes events
Encrypts the stream
questions.explanation: Windowing groups continuous events into intervals (e.g. 5-minute windows) so aggregates can be computed.

questions.q: Batch is often preferred for high 'throughput'. What does throughput mean?
options: The delay per event
The volume of data processed per unit of time
The number of bugs
The cost per query
questions.explanation: Throughput is how much data is processed per unit time; batch excels at processing large volumes efficiently.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses 'exactly-once' processing?
options: Exactly-once means events are dropped.
Exactly-once guarantees each event affects the result one time despite retries.
Exactly-once doubles the data.
It means batch only.
questions.explanation: Exactly-once semantics ensure each event is reflected once, even with failures and retries - a key streaming concern.

questions.q: Code Review Comment During a code review for the new user registration service, Sarah flagged this PR description: "This batch process will pull all new user data from the database every hour and update our CRM. It's simple, fast, and handles large volumes of users."
options: insufficient - the description doesn't address potential issues with data consistency.
correct - the description accurately reflects a common and efficient approach for handling user registration volume.
incorrect - 'batch' implies immediate processing; this should emphasize how data is accumulated over time.
incorrect - the term 'fast' is subjective and doesn't provide any technical justification for choosing batch over streaming.
questions.explanation: The key misunderstanding here lies in equating 'batch' with immediate processing. While a batch process *does* accumulate data, its primary characteristic is that it processes this accumulated data as a single unit at scheduled intervals (hourly in this case). The description accurately highlights the benefits of batch-handling large volumes and simplicity-which are core reasons for choosing this approach when high throughput is needed. Options A, C, and D all misrepresent the fundamental trade-offs associated with batch processing.

questions.q: Sarah commented on the PR description: "This batch process will pull all new user data from the database every hour and update our CRM. It's simple, fast, and handles large volumes of users." Considering Sarah's comment, which statement best describes the primary advantage of using a batch processing approach in this scenario? A : Batch processing guarantees that user data is processed sequentially, ensuring order preservation. B : Batch processing prioritizes minimizing the time between data extraction and CRM update, suitable for real-time updates. C : Batch processing efficiently processes large amounts of data in discrete chunks, often scheduled periodically. D : Batch processing reduces computational load by performing calculations concurrently across multiple machines.
options: A: Batch processing guarantees that user data is processed sequentially, ensuring order preservation.
B: Batch processing prioritizes minimizing the time between data extraction and CRM update, suitable for real-time updates.
C: Batch processing efficiently processes large amounts of data in discrete chunks, often scheduled periodically.
D: Batch processing reduces computational load by performing calculations concurrently across multiple machines.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Sarah's comment highlights the focus on 'fast' and 'large volumes'. Batch processing excels at handling large datasets when immediate reaction isn't crucial; it prioritizes minimizing the time between data extraction from the database and updating the CRM. Options A, C, and D misrepresent key aspects of batch processing - sequential processing is not a defining feature, chunking is relevant but less central than overall throughput, and concurrent computation isn't inherent to the batch model.

questions.q: David from the DevOps team sent this Slack message: "Just finished running a nightly batch job to process all new payment transactions. It took about 30 minutes, but it processed over 10,000 records! We're aiming for similar throughput with our streaming pipeline." What does David primarily mean by 'throughput' in this context?
options: A: The total volume of data processed during a single execution.
B: The speed at which individual transactions are completed.
C: The number of users affected by the processing job.
D: The cost associated with running the batch job.
questions.explanation: Throughput refers to the *rate* at which data is processed-how much data is handled per unit of time. David uses it to highlight the high volume of transactions successfully processed by his batch job. Options B and D relate to different aspects of performance or cost, while options C is irrelevant.

questions.q: Maria is explaining the rationale behind choosing a streaming approach for real-time fraud detection. She states: "We need to react *immediately* when suspicious activity is detected - we can't wait an hour for a batch job to analyze everything." What key characteristic of streaming justifies Maria's decision?
options: A: Streaming prioritizes minimizing the size of individual data records.
B: Streaming minimizes latency and enables real-time responses to events.
C: Streaming is always cheaper than batch processing in terms of infrastructure costs.
D: Streaming simplifies complex data transformations for large datasets.
questions.explanation: Latency - the delay between an event occurring and a response being generated - is crucial when immediate action is required. Maria's statement explicitly emphasizes this need, highlighting that streaming systems are designed to minimize latency for real-time processing. Options A, C, and D address different aspects of data processing but don't explain the core reason behind minimizing delay.

exercises.title: Data Catalog & Governance Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for data lineage, metadata, business glossary, data stewardship, and PII tagging.

questions.q: A data catalog is described as the 'Google search for your data' because:
options: It is built using Google's search technology.

It provides a searchable, indexed inventory of all datasets in an organisation - including metadata, lineage, quality metrics, and business context - so analysts and engineers can discover and understand available data.
It restricts data access in the same way Google restricts certain search results.
It crawls and indexes data from external Google services into the warehouse.
questions.explanation: Data catalogs (Alation, Atlan, DataHub, OpenMetadata) solve data discoverability: without a catalog, analysts don't know what data exists, where it is, what it means, or whether it's trustworthy. A catalog indexes assets and makes them searchable with rich context.

questions.q: A business glossary in a data catalog maps:
options: Technical abbreviations used in database column names to their full names.

Business terms (like 'Customer', 'Revenue', 'Active User') to their precise technical definitions and the specific tables/columns that implement them - bridging the gap between business language and data engineering.
Company-specific jargon used in internal communication to standard industry terms.
Column names across different databases that represent the same business concept.
questions.explanation: Business glossary example: 'Active User' may be defined as 'a user who has logged in at least once in the last 30 days and has completed at least one core action' - with a link to the fact table and the exact query implementing this definition. Without this, different teams use different definitions.

questions.q: Data stewardship refers to:
options: The technical role of maintaining database infrastructure and backups.
The responsibility for ensuring specific data assets are accurate, well-documented, and properly governed - a data steward owns the quality, definition, and usage policy for specific datasets.
The process of archiving old data that is no longer needed in active systems.
The engineering practice of steering data through pipeline stages correctly.
questions.explanation: Data stewards are typically business domain experts (not engineers) who ensure their domain's data is accurate and well-defined. They answer: 'What does this field mean?', 'Who is responsible for its quality?', 'When should this data be deleted?' - bridging business and technical teams.

questions.q: PII tagging in a data catalog means:
options: Adding price tags to commercially valuable datasets.
Marking specific columns or datasets as containing Personally Identifiable Information - enabling automated access controls, retention policies, masking, and GDPR/CCPA right-to-erasure workflows.
Labelling datasets with a 'personally identified' flag when they are accessed by named users.
Tagging individual records in a database that belong to specific users.
questions.explanation: PII tagging drives automated governance: tagged columns can have access restricted to authorised users, can trigger masking in non-production environments, and can be included in automated data deletion workflows for GDPR erasure requests - without engineers having to remember which columns contain personal data.

questions.q: Data discoverability in the context of a data catalog means:
options: The ability to discover new data sources and onboard them to the warehouse.
The ability for analysts and engineers to find the data they need - knowing it exists, understanding what it contains, trusting its quality, and knowing who to ask for help.
Discovering anomalies and quality issues in data that had previously gone unnoticed.
The ability to discover patterns in data using machine learning techniques.
questions.explanation: Poor discoverability creates shadow analytics: analysts build their own spreadsheets because they can't find the official data. A catalog with good metadata, descriptions, popularity signals, and verified owner contact information makes the official data the path of least resistance.

questions.q: An alert fires: "The data pipeline SLA was breached - the reporting dataset was delayed by 4 hours." Which stakeholders must be notified first in a data SLA breach?
options: The data governance committee.
External auditors if the data is subject to regulatory requirements.
Only the data engineering team responsible for the pipeline.
Business stakeholders who depend on the data for time-sensitive decisions (e.g., finance at month-end close, ops teams using daily reports) and the engineering leadership on-call.
questions.explanation: SLA breach communication - who needs to know and when: Notification priority Audience Why urgent Immediate Dependent business consumers + eng leadership They may be acting on stale data right now During incident Regular updates to affected teams Manage expectations, allow workaround Post-resolution All-clear notification + RCA summary Data is safe to use again Message template: what data is affected, issue time, estimated recovery, business impact, any available workaround. Key vocabulary: SLA breach notification , business impact assessment , interim workaround , recovery ETA , impacted stakeholders .

questions.q: During an incident, the team announces: "We are investigating an ingestion failure affecting the events table - data from the last 6 hours may be incomplete. Please treat any reports from that window as preliminary." What communication principle does this statement follow?
options: Root cause analysis - identifying the technical failure before communicating.
Post-mortem format - summarising the incident for leadership review.
Transparent proactive communication - acknowledging the issue, scope, and impact on data consumers before root cause is known.
Minimising communication to reduce panic.
questions.explanation: Data incident communication best practices : Principle Action in the example Acknowledge early "We are investigating" - before root cause known Define affected scope Specific table + 6-hour time window named Warn consumers "Treat reports as preliminary" Never wait for root cause before communicating impact to consumers. Key vocabulary: data incident , impacted time window , preliminary data warning , update cadence , data incident runbook .

questions.q: A post-incident RCA states: "A schema change caused a silent data drop - the pipeline succeeded but records were missing." What does "silent data drop" mean in a data pipeline context?
options: The pipeline completed in silent mode with logging disabled.
Data was lost without any pipeline error - the job succeeded but silently filtered out or failed to ingest some records.
The database audit log was disabled during the incident.
A network timeout caused individual records to be dropped.
questions.explanation: Silent data drop - one of the hardest data incidents to detect: Type What happened Detection method Silent drop Pipeline exit code 0, but rows are missing Row count monitoring, reconciliation Explicit failure Error raised, pipeline stopped Error alerts, monitoring dashboards Common causes: new NOT NULL column rejected rows silently, schema mismatch filtering, API pagination bug. Key vocabulary: silent failure , data loss without error , quality check gate , expected vs. actual row count check .

questions.q: An incident resolution message reads: "The data team will perform a backfill for the affected date range." What does a backfill involve in data engineering?
options: Reverting the pipeline to the last working version.
Copying data from a backup snapshot to replace the corrupted tables.
Deleting and re-inserting the affected data partition with corrected records.
Re-running the pipeline for historical date ranges to populate missing or incorrect data - overwriting the affected partitions with the corrected result.
questions.explanation: Backfill = run pipeline for past time periods to fill gaps or correct errors: Backfill concept Explanation Idempotent backfill Re-running produces the same result (uses WRITE_TRUNCATE or UPSERT) Backfill window The date range being re-processed Incremental backfill Re-process day by day to control cost/load Key vocabulary: backfill window , idempotent backfill , backfill schedule , incremental backfill , cost of full historical backfill .

questions.q: A post-mortem action item reads: "Add a row count check gate that fails the pipeline if ingested rows differ from expected by more than 5%." What type of data reliability improvement does this represent?
options: Proactive data observability - adding automated quality gates to catch anomalies before data reaches consumers.
Data governance compliance enforcement.
Data lineage improvement.
Pipeline performance optimisation.
questions.explanation: Data observability = monitoring data health in production: Observability pillar What it monitors Freshness Is data up-to-date? Volume Is row count within expected range? (this action) Schema Did column names/types change unexpectedly? Distribution Are value distributions normal? This action adds a volume anomaly detection gate. Key vocabulary: data observability , quality gate , row count SLO , anomaly detection threshold , shift-left data quality .

questions.q: You're a DevOps engineer and receive the following Slack message from your data team: 'Urgent: We've detected a potential issue with the customer transaction data. The API endpoint returns a 500 error intermittently, and we're seeing increased latency in queries against that table. Initial investigation suggests it might be related to recent schema changes.' Which of the following is the MOST appropriate immediate response to this message, considering your role and responsibilities?
options: 'Okay, thanks for the update. Let the data team handle it.'
'Can you please provide more details about the schema changes and their impact? What's the current status of the investigation?'
'Just monitor the error rate - it will likely resolve itself.'
questions.explanation: The correct response acknowledges the issue and requests further information to understand the scope and potential impact. The other options are insufficient because they don't actively participate in assessing the situation or directing the investigation. Asking about schema changes is crucial as these often trigger unexpected data behavior, and understanding the current status allows for timely escalation if needed. It's important to shift from passive observation to active engagement in a critical incident.

questions.q: During an incident investigation, the monitoring system alerts you to a sudden spike in HTTP 503 errors originating from your customer-facing API. Initial analysis suggests a potential resource exhaustion issue. Which of the following actions should be prioritized first?
options: Rollback the recent deployment of the API to restore service stability.
Immediately escalate to the CISO for security implications.
Investigate the root cause - is there a sudden surge in legitimate traffic, or an unexpected spike in requests from bots?
Notify all development teams of the outage for immediate support.
questions.explanation: The primary goal is to understand *why* the errors are occurring before taking drastic action. A 503 error often indicates resource limits - investigating traffic patterns or bot activity will help determine if this is a legitimate issue or a symptom of a larger problem. Rollbacks should be reserved for later stages after understanding the cause.

questions.q: You're reviewing a code change that adds logging to a critical data transformation process. The developer has added `console.log()` statements throughout the function but hasn't included any filtering or sanitization of the log output. What is the MOST important concern you should raise during the review?
options: That the code is not well-documented.
The inefficient use of memory during the logging process.
The potential for exposing sensitive data in the logs, such as Personally Identifiable Information (PII).
The lack of unit tests to verify the correct operation of the transformation.
questions.explanation: While documentation and testing are important, the immediate risk is data leakage. Unsanitized logs can expose sensitive information - this is a critical security concern. Focusing on log filtering/sanitization should be the top priority in this review.

questions.q: A colleague sends you this Slack message: 'Our nightly data sync failed again - we're seeing a lot of 'connection refused' errors. The logs show the database server is unreachable.' What's your *immediate* response to this message?
options: 'Sounds like a network issue; check your firewall settings.'
'That's just how it is with data pipelines - they sometimes fail.'
'Did anyone change anything recently?'.
'Okay, let's investigate the database server status and network connectivity. Can you share the relevant logs?'
questions.explanation: The message highlights a specific error and potential cause. A productive response involves confirming the issue, requesting more information (logs), and initiating an investigation. Simply stating a generic solution or dismissing the problem isn't helpful.

questions.q: You're drafting the PR description for a change that updates the schema of a large data warehouse table. The description includes the following sentence: 'This update will improve query performance.' What additional information should you *definitely* include in the PR description to ensure transparency and facilitate rollback if needed?
options: The specific queries that were identified as slow, the estimated performance improvement (e.g., 'reduced query execution time by 20%'), and a clear rollback plan if the change introduces issues.
A summary of the data validation steps performed after the update.
A link to the documentation for the new schema design.
The names of the developers who worked on the PR.
questions.explanation: Simply stating that the change improves performance is insufficient. Quantifying the improvement (if possible), outlining the rollback strategy, and detailing the validation steps are crucial for accountability and risk mitigation during a schema update - especially in large data warehouses.

questions.q: During your daily stand-up, you report: 'I'm currently working on implementing a new automated retry mechanism for failed API calls to our third-party data provider. The goal is to improve the resilience of our data ingestion pipeline.' Which aspect of this update is MOST important to highlight to the team?
options: The configuration details of the third-party API.
The potential impact on latency if the retry mechanism introduces delays.
The number of lines of code you have written.
The specific programming language you are using (e.g., Python).
questions.explanation: While technical details are relevant, the core focus during a stand-up is communicating the *impact* of your work. Highlighting potential latency implications ensures everyone understands the trade-offs and that it doesn't negatively affect other services.

exercises.title: Data Pipeline Orchestration
exercises.subtitle: Learn the IT-English vocabulary of data pipeline orchestration: DAGs, scheduling, dependencies, backfills and retries.

questions.q: An orchestrator models the pipeline as a 'DAG'. What does DAG stand for?
options: Data Aggregation Group
Directed Acyclic Graph - tasks with dependencies and no cycles
Database Access Gateway
Daily Automated Job
questions.explanation: A DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) defines task order via dependencies without any loops.

questions.q: A task is 'downstream' of another. What does that mean?
options: It runs first
It depends on and runs after the upstream task completes
It is unrelated
It runs on another server
questions.explanation: Downstream tasks wait for their upstream dependencies to finish before they run.

questions.q: The team runs a 'backfill'. What is it?
options: Deleting old data
Re-running the pipeline over a past time range to populate or correct historical data
A live stream
A schema change
questions.explanation: A backfill processes historical periods, e.g. after fixing a bug or adding a new table.

questions.q: A task has a 'retry policy' of 3 attempts. What does that achieve?
options: It runs 3 pipelines
Transient failures are automatically re-attempted before the task is marked failed
It triples the data
It disables the task
questions.explanation: Retries handle transient errors (e.g. a brief network blip) without manual intervention.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses 'idempotent' for a pipeline task?
options: Idempotent means it runs faster.
Make the load step idempotent so re-running it doesn't duplicate rows.
Idempotent means it fails twice.
It means encrypted output.
questions.explanation: An idempotent task produces the same result if re-run, which is essential for safe retries and backfills.

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I've just submitted a PR to update the data validation logic in our ingestion pipeline. It should handle cases where some records are missing from the source system. The orchestrator is running the new task as a downstream step after the initial ETL job."
options: The orchestrator is now responsible for proactively monitoring the health of the entire data flow.
The orchestration model defines a dependency chain, and this task's execution relies on the successful completion of the preceding ETL step.
Sarah is suggesting we manually trigger the data validation job every hour to ensure data quality.
This indicates that Sarah has moved the source system directly into the pipeline for immediate processing.
questions.explanation: Downstream in a data pipeline refers to tasks that depend on the successful completion of preceding tasks. The orchestrator manages this dependency chain; it doesn't proactively monitor health or trigger jobs manually. Sarah's statement correctly describes a downstream task's execution relying on the ETL job's output, which is a core concept of DAG-based orchestration. The wrong options misinterpret the role of the orchestrator and the nature of dependency in data pipelines.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'I'm seeing a lot of implicit dependencies here. The `transform_data` task relies on the output of `extract_data`, but there isn't an explicit dependency declared in the orchestrator model. This makes it difficult to understand the order of execution and potentially introduces race conditions if those tasks run concurrently. Consider adding a dag.directed_edge to ensure proper ordering.'
options: A: A directed graph is simply a visual representation of the data flow, with no specific implications for task dependencies.

B: A dag.directed_edge defines an explicit dependency between two tasks in the pipeline, ensuring that one task completes before another can begin execution - this helps prevent unintended parallelization and ensures correct processing order.
C: Implicit dependencies are always preferable in orchestrator models as they allow for greater flexibility and dynamic adaptation to changing data volumes.
D: Race conditions only occur when multiple users simultaneously access the same database, not within a data pipeline orchestrated by an external tool.
questions.explanation: The question tests understanding of how orchestrators manage task dependencies. exercises.title: Data Quality Monitoring
exercises.subtitle: Master the IT-English vocabulary of data quality monitoring: freshness, completeness, validation checks, anomalies and data contracts.

questions.q: A monitor checks data 'freshness'. What does freshness measure?
options: How tasty the data is
How recently the data was updated versus expectations
The number of columns
The file format
questions.explanation: Freshness checks whether data arrived/updated within the expected time window.

questions.q: A 'completeness' check flags many null values. What is completeness?
options: The disk usage
Whether expected data is present rather than missing
The query speed
The encryption level
questions.explanation: Completeness measures whether all expected records and fields are present, not missing or null.

questions.q: A 'data contract' is agreed between producer and consumer. What does it define?
options: The salary
The expected schema, types and guarantees of the data so changes don't silently break consumers
The server location
The retry count
questions.explanation: A data contract formalises schema and quality expectations so producers can't break consumers unexpectedly.

questions.q: A monitor detects a row-count 'anomaly'. What does that suggest?
options: The data is encrypted
The volume deviates sharply from the norm, hinting at a pipeline problem
The schema improved
The data is fresh
questions.explanation: A volume anomaly (e.g. a sudden drop) often signals an upstream failure or partial load.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses 'validation rule'?
options: A validation rule is a chart type.
A validation rule asserts that order_total is never negative.
A validation rule speeds up loads.
It is a server name.
questions.explanation: A validation rule is an assertion the data must satisfy; violations raise alerts.

questions.q: PR Description: "Fix: Updated user profile data. Added new fields for 'preferred_timezone' and 'communication_preference'. Ran initial data quality checks." During a code review, Sarah asks, "What does 'data quality' mean in this context? Are we just checking that the new fields exist, or is there more to it?", which of the following best describes her concern?
options: insufficient - the PR doesn't include any data quality checks themselves.
correct - the description simply indicates that new fields were added and initial checks were performed.
incorrect - 'data quality' solely refers to ensuring the new fields are present in the database schema.
incorrect - 'data quality' should also encompass verifying the accuracy, completeness, and consistency of the newly added data.
questions.explanation: Sarah's question highlights a crucial aspect of data quality beyond just field existence. 'Data quality' encompasses much more than simply confirming that new fields are present; it demands verification of their *accuracy* (do the values make sense?), *completeness* (are all required fields populated?), and *consistency* (are the values compatible across different systems?). The PR description only scratches the surface - a truly robust data quality check would involve validating these dimensions.

options: Data completeness - ensuring all expected fields are populated.
Data accuracy - verifying that existing values are correct.
Data freshness - assessing how recently the data was updated.
Data consistency - checking if values align across different datasets.
questions.explanation: Alex is focused on data completeness , which refers to the proportion of records containing all required fields. While accuracy, freshness, and consistency are important aspects of data quality, Alex's message explicitly highlights the absence of `customer_segment` values, directly addressing whether the dataset has sufficient information. The Slack channel suggests a need for immediate action to address this issue.

questions.q: During a standup meeting, Mark says: 'We've implemented a new data quality check in the pipeline that flags rows with `order_total` values exceeding $10,000. We're using the SQLAlchemy library to perform this validation.' What type of data quality issue is Mark describing?
options: Data drift - changes in the distribution of data over time.
Data schema violation - a mismatch between the expected and actual structure of the data.
Anomaly detection - identifying unusual or unexpected values within the dataset.
Constraint validation - enforcing rules that limit the range or type of acceptable data.
questions.explanation: Mark is describing constraint validation . This involves defining rules (in this case, a maximum order total) to ensure data falls within acceptable limits. Anomaly detection would identify outliers, schema violations are about structure, and data drift concerns changes over time - none of which align with the described scenario. Using SQLAlchemy for this check is standard practice.

questions.q: David writes in a PR description: 'Implemented data quality checks to ensure all product IDs in the inventory database are valid UUIDs. This prevents errors when synchronizing with our e-commerce platform.' What is David's primary goal in this change?
options: Data transformation - converting data from one format to another.
Data standardization - ensuring data adheres to a consistent format and structure.
Data type validation - verifying that data conforms to its expected data type.
Data enrichment - adding additional information to existing data.
questions.explanation: David is focused on data standardization . Validating product IDs as UUIDs ensures they adhere to a specific, pre-defined format and structure. This is crucial for reliable synchronization with the e-commerce platform. Data transformation, enrichment, and type validation are not the primary focus of this particular PR description.

questions.q: A monitoring system detects a significant increase in the number of records with `user_age` values outside the range of 18-65. What is the most likely underlying issue being flagged?
options: Data skew - uneven distribution of data around its mean.
Data corruption - damage to the integrity of the database records.
Data inconsistency - conflicting values across different datasets.
Data validation failure - a rule or constraint has been violated.
questions.explanation: The increase in `user_age` values outside the specified range indicates a data validation failure . This suggests that either the data entry process is flawed (e.g., incorrect input) or that a validation rule was not properly enforced during data ingestion. Data skew and corruption are less likely given the specific value range.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of using a 'golden record' in data quality monitoring?
options: To identify all records with errors - flagging every instance of invalid data.
To create a single, trusted version of truth - representing the most accurate and complete information for a specific entity.
To automatically correct data inconsistencies - resolving conflicting values across different systems.
To generate reports on data quality metrics - tracking key performance indicators related to data accuracy.
questions.explanation: A 'golden record' represents the single, most accurate and complete version of a specific entity's data. This is achieved by merging and resolving inconsistencies from multiple source systems. Identifying all errors (option A) is too broad; automatic correction (option C) isn't the primary goal, and reporting metrics (option D) are a result of having a golden record, not its purpose.

questions.q: A data quality dashboard shows a 2.3% null rate on a required field . Which data quality dimension does this violate?
options: Accuracy - the data does not match the real world.
Completeness - required fields must be populated; missing values indicate incomplete data.
Consistency - the data disagrees with a related system.
Timeliness - the data has not been refreshed on schedule.
questions.explanation: Data quality dimensions (DAMA framework): Dimension Question it answers Example violation Completeness Are all required values present? 2.3% null rate on required field Accuracy Does data match reality? Wrong address on customer record Timeliness Is data fresh enough for use? Report uses yesterday's data Consistency Same values across systems? CRM and warehouse disagree on revenue Key vocabulary: null rate , completeness check , required vs. optional fields , data quality threshold .

questions.q: A pipeline has a Great Expectations suite checking for data validity. What does "data validity" mean as a quality dimension?
options: The data originates from an approved source system.
The data has been reviewed by a data steward.
The data conforms to defined format, range, type, and business rules - e.g., age must be between 0 and 150, email must match a regex pattern.
The data was loaded without errors.
questions.explanation: Validity = data meets defined business rules and constraints: Validity check type Example rule Range validation age BETWEEN 0 AND 150 Format check Date must match YYYY-MM-DD Enum constraint status IN ('active', 'inactive', 'pending') Regex pattern Email must match ^[\w.]+@[\w.]+$ Tools: Great Expectations expectations, dbt tests (accepted_values, not_null, relationships). Key vocabulary: constraint check , range validation , regex pattern check , referential integrity check .

questions.q: A data monitoring alert fires: "Row count dropped from 1.2M to 890K yesterday." In data monitoring, what does a sudden drop in row count typically signal?
options: A pipeline failure, data source issue, or ingestion gap - requires investigation to rule out production data loss.
The data warehouse auto-compressed old rows.
A scheduled maintenance window that paused ingestion.
Normal statistical variation within expected ranges.
questions.explanation: Row count anomaly detection - a fundamental data monitoring check: Anomaly type Likely cause Sudden drop in row count Pipeline failure, source API issue, schema change filtering rows Sudden spike in row count Duplicate ingestion, re-processing of historical data Gradual decline Source system usage decline or data sourcing issue Key vocabulary: data volume anomaly , ingestion failure , row count SLO , anomaly detection threshold , data observability (Monte Carlo, Anomalo) .

questions.q: An engineer says: "The data contract between the producer team and the consumer team was violated." What is a data contract ?
options: A formal schema and quality agreement between the producer (data source team) and consumer (data user team) - specifying field names, types, nullability, freshness, and expected volume.
An SLA document specifying data delivery timelines.
A legal agreement between companies sharing data.
A GDPR data processing agreement.
questions.explanation: Data contracts = producer-consumer agreement on data structure and behaviour: Contract element What it defines Schema Field names, types, nullability Freshness SLO How recent the data must be Volume expectations Expected row count ranges Prevents: "the upstream team changed a field name and broke my pipeline". Key vocabulary: schema contract , breaking schema change , producer obligations , consumer expectations , contract versioning .

questions.q: A data reconciliation job reports: "0.4% discrepancy found between the source system and the warehouse." What is data reconciliation ?
options: Comparing counts and aggregates between source systems and the data warehouse to verify data was ingested accurately and completely.
Merging duplicate records across data sources.
Deleting stale data from expired partitions.
Correcting historical data errors retroactively.
questions.explanation: Reconciliation = source vs. target comparison to verify complete, accurate ingestion: Reconciliation check What it verifies Row count match Same number of records source vs. warehouse Aggregate match sum(revenue) matches between systems No dropped rows No records lost or duplicated in transit Discrepancy investigation: trace which pipeline stage introduced the difference. Key vocabulary: source-to-target reconciliation , reconciliation threshold (acceptable error %) , discrepancy investigation , audit count check .

Update the current customer row in-place with new values.

questions.q: PR Description: "Implemented a new ETL process to load daily sales data into the data warehouse. Utilizing Slowly Changing Dimension (SCD) Type 1 for product updates and incremental loading based on date." During code review, your team lead asks: 'Can you elaborate on why we used SCD Type 1 here? What are the potential downsides?'
options: It's the most efficient method for handling large datasets due to its minimal data modification.
SCD Type 1 is suitable when historical changes to dimension attributes are not important and only the current state needs to be preserved, minimizing storage requirements.
SCD Type 1 guarantees a complete audit trail of all product changes over time, allowing for precise historical analysis.
SCD Type 1 automatically handles concurrent updates from multiple sources, eliminating data conflicts.
questions.explanation: SCD Type 1 is the most appropriate choice in this scenario because it focuses on maintaining a current snapshot of dimension attributes without capturing historical changes. The key advantage is simplicity and efficiency for situations where historical accuracy isn't paramount - a common use case when loading new data daily. Options A, B, and C misrepresent the core functionality or potential drawbacks of SCD Type 1; it doesn't guarantee audit trails or handle concurrent updates natively.

questions.q: // Code Review Comment Your team lead is reviewing a recent PR and asks: 'Can you elaborate on why we used SCD Type 1 here? What are the potential downsides?' Consider this snippet of code as context: ```sql INSERT INTO sales_fact (sale_id, product_key, customer_key, date_key, quantity, price) VALUES (12345, 9876, 5432, '2023-10-26', 2, 19.99); ``` Which of the following best describes a key limitation of using SCD Type 1 in this scenario?
options: It allows for tracking complex historical changes to product attributes with multiple versions simultaneously.
It doesn't capture any changes to dimension attributes, resulting in a simplified view but potentially inaccurate reporting over time if the original value is no longer representative.
SCD Type 1 automatically handles all data type conversions and ensures consistency across different fact tables.
It's primarily designed for handling large volumes of transactional data, offering superior performance compared to other SCD types.
questions.explanation: SCD Type 1 is the simplest approach, replacing old values with new ones when a dimension attribute changes. This means it *doesn't* track historical versions; if a product's color changed from 'red' to 'blue', the `product_key` in the `sales_fact` table would simply be updated to reflect the new value. The primary downside is that this creates an inaccurate record of the past, as the original, correct value is lost - a critical consideration for reporting and analysis where historical accuracy is paramount. Options A, C, and D are incorrect because they describe features of other SCD types or unrelated aspects of data warehousing.

questions.q: Mark, a senior data engineer, is discussing SCD Type 1 with the team. He states: 'SCD Type 1 allows us to track changes to attributes but doesn't capture the history of those changes.' What does this statement primarily highlight about SCD Type 1?
questions.explanation: SCD Type 1 is designed for simplicity. It adds a 'valid from' and 'valid to' column to represent changes to attributes like customer address. However, it *doesn't* retain the historical values of those changed attributes; once the 'valid to' date passes, the old value is overwritten with the new one. This is a deliberate design choice for performance reasons.

A formal specification of the model's schema (column names, types, constraints) and quality expectations - enforced by dbt tests and contracts features - guaranteeing downstream consumers a stable, predictable interface.
An external API specification published alongside the dbt project.

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I'm getting a lot of warnings in the dbt run logs about 'invalid column name'. It seems like some of our source tables are using backticks for identifiers, but we're not doing that in our models. Should I add a transformation to normalize those names?"
options: incorrect - the warnings are simply a reminder to double-check that all columns in our dbt models match the exact naming conventions of the source tables.
correct - normalizing column names will resolve the 'invalid column name' warnings and improve model consistency.
insufficient - the issue is likely a typo in the source data.

incorrect - adding transformations to normalize column names will break the existing dbt models and potentially introduce new errors. The warnings suggest an underlying problem with the source data itself .
questions.explanation: This scenario reflects a common issue when connecting to sources where backticks are used for identifiers. The 'invalid column name' warning indicates a mismatch between the expected naming convention in dbt (typically without backticks) and the actual names in the source tables. Adding transformations to normalize these names is a valid solution, but it's important to investigate *why* the sources use backticks initially - this might point to a deeper problem with data governance or upstream tooling that needs addressing. The key here is understanding the root cause of the warning, not just applying a blanket transformation.

questions.q: During a code review of a dbt model, Alex comments: 'I'm seeing that this model is relying heavily on the {{ ref('stg_customers') }} expression. While it works, are we sure this isn't an anti-pattern? Shouldn't we be explicitly defining how we want to join data from the staging layer rather than implicitly through a reference?' What is Alex raising concerns about regarding the use of `ref()` in this scenario?
options: B. Relying solely on ref() can create tight coupling between models and obscure the data transformation logic, potentially leading to unexpected behavior if the staging layer changes.
A. The ref() function automatically handles all upstream dependencies, ensuring optimal performance.
D. Using ref() always guarantees that the latest version of the staging table is used, regardless of dbt's caching mechanism.
C. The ref() function is only suitable for referencing simple, one-to-one relationships between tables.
questions.explanation: Alex's concern highlights a potential anti-pattern: excessive reliance on `ref()` without explicit data transformation logic. While `ref()` simplifies dependency management by automatically updating references to upstream models, it can make the model less understandable and more susceptible to issues if the staging layer changes unexpectedly. Explicitly defining joins and transformations promotes maintainability and reduces coupling - a core principle of robust dbt development. Option C is incorrect because caching mechanisms are designed to mitigate this issue.

questions.q: Liam (Senior Developer) posts this comment on a PR describing a new dbt model: "I've reviewed the `fct_sales` model. The use of `{{ lookup('auto', 'sales') }}` feels a bit verbose. Could we explore using a CTE to simplify this and improve readability? Also, are we sure that relying on `auto` for the entire sales table is the best approach - perhaps we should explicitly define the columns we need?"
options: auto is a dbt-specific function and shouldn't be used.
auto automatically handles data type conversions, which improves performance.
insufficient - the query is running too slowly
auto is an efficient way to fetch all columns from the `sales` table, but Liam's concerns about readability and potential simplification are valid.
questions.explanation: Liam's comment highlights important considerations regarding dbt's `lookup()` function. While auto is a convenient way to fetch an entire table, it can lead to less readable queries and potentially unnecessary data retrieval if only specific columns are needed. CTEs (Common Table Expressions) offer a cleaner and more maintainable approach for complex transformations, allowing developers to explicitly define the required columns and improve query readability. The key takeaway is that dbt encourages efficient and well-structured SQL, and Liam's feedback aims to achieve this.

I've added a `materialized = deferred` setting, but it's still slow when running reports. Any ideas?' Alice suggests: 'Have you considered using a `unique` constraint on the `customer_id` column in your dbt model? This can significantly speed up queries by preventing redundant scans.' What is the primary benefit of adding a unique constraint to a dbt model, as suggested by Alice?
options: A. It automatically indexes the customer_id column for faster lookups.
B. It enforces data quality by ensuring no duplicate customer IDs are present in the model.
C. It allows dbt to optimize query plans by avoiding full table scans when filtering on customer_id .
D. It prevents the dbt compiler from generating inefficient SQL queries related to customer_id .
questions.explanation: The unique constraint forces dbt and the database engine to optimize query plans more effectively. When a filter is applied on customer_id , the database can avoid full table scans because it knows there are no duplicates-this drastically reduces query execution time. Options A and D misrepresent how constraints influence query optimization; B focuses on data quality, not performance directly, and C is too general. Adding a unique constraint triggers index creation or suggests more efficient indexing strategies.

The key takeaway is that dbt encourages efficient and well-structured SQL, and Liam's feedback aims to achieve this.

questions.q: During a Slack conversation about optimizing a dbt model, Ben says: 'I'm trying to make the `fct_orders` model faster. I've added a `materialized = deferred` setting, but it's still slow when running reports. Any ideas?' Alice suggests: 'Have you considered using a `unique` constraint on the `customer_id` column in your dbt model? This can significantly speed up queries by preventing redundant scans.' What is the primary benefit of adding a unique constraint to a dbt model, as suggested by Alice?
options: A. It automatically indexes the customer_id column for faster lookups.
B. It enforces data quality by ensuring no duplicate customer IDs are present in the model.
C. It allows dbt to optimize query plans by avoiding full table scans when filtering on customer_id .
D. It prevents the dbt compiler from generating inefficient SQL queries related to customer_id .
questions.explanation: The unique constraint forces dbt and the database engine to optimize query plans more effectively. When a filter is applied on customer_id , the database can avoid full table scans because it knows there are no duplicates-this drastically reduces query execution time. Options A and D misrepresent how constraints influence query optimization; B focuses on data quality, not performance directly, and C is too general. Adding a unique constraint triggers index creation or suggests more efficient indexing strategies.

questions.q: During a standup update, David says: 'We're using dbt's `select` macro to filter our sales data based on specific criteria. It's great because we can easily control exactly which columns are included in the final mart table.' Maria asks, 'But what happens if the source tables change and new columns appear? Will our select macro automatically adapt?' What potential challenge is Maria highlighting regarding using the `select` macro in this way?
options: The select macro's reliance on static column definitions makes it inflexible and vulnerable to changes in upstream source tables, potentially leading to broken downstream models.
Maria's concern is irrelevant; dbt automatically handles schema evolution regardless of the select macro's configuration.
Insufficient - the sales data volume is too high to efficiently process with a complex select statement.
Using a select macro is perfectly acceptable for filtering sales data as long as the user manually updates it whenever source table changes occur.
questions.explanation: Maria correctly identifies a key vulnerability: the `select` macro's static nature. dbt's transformations, particularly those relying on macros like this, don't inherently adapt to schema evolution in upstream tables without manual intervention. This can lead to broken downstream models if source columns are added or renamed unexpectedly, highlighting the need for more robust change management strategies within the data stack.

exercises.title: ETL vs ELT Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practise the vocabulary for ETL, ELT, Change Data Capture (CDC), and incremental vs full load patterns.

questions.q: The key difference between ETL and ELT is:
options: ETL is for streaming data; ELT is for batch data processing.
ETL transforms data before loading it into the destination; ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse using its compute power.
ETL is the newer approach; ELT is the legacy pattern.
ETL requires a separate transformation server; ELT transforms in the source system.
questions.explanation: ETL (legacy): transform → load using a dedicated transformation layer (Informatica, Talend). ELT (modern): load raw data into a cloud warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery), then transform in-warehouse using SQL/dbt. ELT became feasible as cloud warehouses gained massive compute at low cost.

questions.q: Change Data Capture (CDC) is used when:
options: You need to capture all changes to a configuration file over time.
You want to synchronise only the rows that have been inserted, updated, or deleted in the source system since the last extraction - rather than copying the full table each time.
You need to capture changes in your data schema between warehouse versions.
You want to detect anomalies in the data quality of your pipeline outputs.
questions.explanation: CDC captures the delta (changes only), reducing data transfer volume and enabling near-real-time replication. Common methods: log-based CDC (reads database transaction logs - Debezium), trigger-based CDC, and timestamp-based incremental extraction.

questions.q: An incremental load in a data pipeline means:
options: The pipeline runs in increments - one table at a time rather than all tables simultaneously.
Only new or changed records since the last successful run are extracted and loaded - identified by a timestamp, updated_at column, or sequence ID.
The pipeline loads data into temporary tables before merging into final tables.
The load process is paused periodically to manage resource consumption.
questions.explanation: Incremental loads are more efficient than full loads for large tables: only the delta is processed. Requires a reliable changed-at timestamp or CDC. Challenge: deleted records are invisible to incremental loads - soft deletes or CDC are needed to handle them.

questions.q: An upsert operation in a data warehouse refers to:
options: Inserting data at the top of a partitioned table for better query performance.
Merging new data into an existing table: inserting new records that don't exist yet, and updating existing records where the data has changed - a combination of UPDATE and INSERT.
Uploading a large batch of data as a single transaction.
Reversing a failed load by removing records that were incorrectly inserted.
questions.explanation: Upsert (MERGE/UPDATE-INSERT) is essential for incremental loads: avoid duplicates from new records while keeping existing records current. SQL: MERGE INTO target USING source ON target.id = source.id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT...

questions.q: The phrase 'ELT became feasible as cloud warehouses gained compute power' means:
options: Cloud warehouses eventually gained the ability to run ETL transformations for free.

Traditional ETL required expensive dedicated transformation servers; cloud warehouses like BigQuery and Snowflake have elastic compute that runs SQL transformations cheaply at scale, making in-warehouse transformation viable.
ELT was invented alongside cloud computing and was always the dominant approach.
ELT became popular because cloud warehouses cannot handle the complex transformations that ETL systems support.
questions.explanation: The ELT shift: cloud DWH pricing (pay-per-query, auto-scaling) made it cheaper to run transformations in the warehouse than to provision and maintain ETL transformation infrastructure. dbt democratised ELT by letting analysts write transformations in SQL.

questions.q: Data lineage in a data engineering context means:
options: The history of who has accessed a particular dataset.

The record of where data originated and how it has been transformed as it flows through pipelines - enabling teams to trace an output back to its source and understand what transformations were applied.
The genetic lineage of a data model, tracing its schema evolution over time.
The line of ownership and stewardship for a dataset within an organisation.
questions.explanation: Data lineage answers: 'Where did this number come from?' If a revenue figure looks wrong, lineage lets you trace it back through transformations to the source tables and identify where the error was introduced. Tools: OpenLineage, Marquez, dbt lineage graph, modern data catalogs.

exercises.title: Data Lakehouse Architecture Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for data lakes, lakehouses, medallion architecture, Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and ACID transactions.

questions.q: The medallion architecture (bronze/silver/gold layers) organises data as:
options: Three separate databases with increasing levels of security classification.

Bronze = raw ingested data (as-is from sources); Silver = cleaned, validated, conformed data; Gold = business-ready aggregations and serving models - each layer adds progressively more quality and refinement.
Three performance tiers: bronze for cold storage, silver for warm, gold for hot queries.
A vendor-specific framework used only with Databricks Delta Lake.
questions.explanation: Medallion architecture progressively improves data quality: Bronze stores source-faithful raw data (audit, replay). Silver applies cleansing, deduplication, type casting, and joins. Gold produces business-level aggregations optimised for specific use cases (finance reporting, product analytics).

questions.q: A data lakehouse combines a data lake and a data warehouse by:
options: Physically merging a data lake storage system with a data warehouse into one product.

Adding structured table formats (Delta Lake, Iceberg, Hudi) on top of cheap object storage - providing ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and SQL query performance typically associated with warehouses, while retaining the low-cost scalable storage of data lakes.
Using a data warehouse as the storage layer and a data lake as the compute layer.
Allowing both structured and unstructured data to coexist in the same warehouse tables.
questions.explanation: The lakehouse pattern: data stored as Parquet files in S3/ADLS/GCS, with a metadata layer (Delta Lake transaction log, Iceberg catalog) providing ACID guarantees, schema evolution, and time travel. Query engines (Spark, Trino, DuckDB) read from object storage directly.

questions.q: ACID transactions in a lakehouse context (Delta Lake, Iceberg) provide:
options: Acid-resistant storage that protects data from corruption.

Atomicity (all-or-nothing writes), Consistency (valid state transitions), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), and Durability (committed data persists) - enabling safe concurrent writes and reads on top of object storage that natively lacks these guarantees.
Advanced Columnar Indexing and Distribution - a compression technique for Parquet files.
Authentication, Authorisation, Cryptography, and Integrity checks for lakehouse security.
questions.explanation: Object storage (S3) has no transaction support: concurrent writers can corrupt each other's data. Delta Lake and Iceberg add a transaction log (DeltaLog / Iceberg metadata) that serialises writes, enabling safe concurrent operations that plain Parquet-on-S3 cannot support.

questions.q: Time travel in Delta Lake or Apache Iceberg allows:
options: Scheduling pipeline runs at specific times in the past to backfill historical data.

Querying a table as it existed at a previous point in time or transaction version - enabling audit, debugging, accidental-deletion recovery, and reproducible ML feature generation from historical snapshots.
Automatically migrating data pipelines when the schema changes over time.
Moving data between storage tiers based on the age of the records.
questions.explanation: Time travel example: SELECT * FROM orders VERSION AS OF 5 or SELECT * FROM orders TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-01-15'. Delta Lake retains transaction log history; Iceberg retains metadata snapshots. Both enable reproducing the exact data state at any past point.

questions.q: Schema-on-read (data lake) compared to schema-on-write (data warehouse) means:
options: Schema-on-read applies the schema during query execution; schema-on-write enforces the schema when data is written - in a data lake, raw data is stored without schema validation, allowing flexible ingestion at the cost of query-time schema complexity.
Schema-on-read is faster because no schema check occurs; schema-on-write is slower but produces cleaner data.
Schema-on-read uses JSON; schema-on-write uses Parquet.
Schema-on-read is used for streaming data; schema-on-write is used for batch data.
questions.explanation: Data lake (schema-on-read): ingest anything, figure out the schema when querying - flexible ingestion, complex queries. Data warehouse (schema-on-write): enforce schema on insert - guaranteed data quality, simpler queries. Lakehouses bridge this: store like a lake, query like a warehouse.

questions.q: A colleague says: "The team migrated from ETL to ELT after moving to Snowflake." What is the key architectural difference between ETL and ELT?
options: ETL requires Hadoop; ELT requires cloud infrastructure.
ETL transforms data before loading it into the destination; ELT loads raw data first, then transforms it inside the data warehouse using its compute.
ETL supports real-time streaming; ELT is batch-only.
ETL uses SQL only; ELT uses Python.
questions.explanation: ETL vs. ELT - the critical architectural distinction: Pattern Flow Where transformation happens ETL Extract → Transform → Load In a separate pipeline/tool before writing to warehouse ELT Extract → Load → Transform Inside the data warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake) using its native compute ELT became practical with scalable cloud DW compute - raw data lands in a "raw zone" first, then SQL/dbt transforms it into a "refined zone". Key vocabulary: transformation layer , raw zone vs. refined zone , dbt for ELT transformations , warehouse-native compute .

questions.q: A data engineer explains: "The data pipeline ingests events in micro-batches every 30 seconds." How does this differ from true "real-time streaming" ?
options: Micro-batching is only available in Spark Structured Streaming.
There is no meaningful difference between micro-batch and streaming for most use cases.
Micro-batching = small batches processed on a short fixed interval; real-time streaming = each event processed as it arrives, with sub-second latency.
Micro-batching requires Kafka; real-time streaming uses REST APIs.
questions.explanation: Streaming vocabulary - understanding latency tiers: Approach Latency Example tools Micro-batch 1-30 second windows Spark Structured Streaming True streaming Per-event, sub-second Apache Flink, Kafka Streams Key vocabulary: event-driven processing , windowing , event time vs. processing time , watermark , late data handling .

questions.q: The pipeline orchestrator shows a failed DAG run . What is a DAG in data pipeline orchestration?
options: A type of data schema used in NoSQL databases.
A Directed Acyclic Graph - a pipeline structure where tasks have dependencies and execution flows in one direction without cycles.
A file format for storing pipeline configurations.
A database audit log for tracking data changes.
questions.explanation: DAG = Directed Acyclic Graph . In orchestration tools (Airflow, Prefect, Dagster): DAG concept Meaning Nodes Tasks (e.g., extract, transform, load steps) Edges Dependencies between tasks Acyclic No cycles - execution flows forward only Failed DAG run At least one task in the pipeline failed Key vocabulary: task dependency , upstream/downstream task , DAG run , trigger rule , SLA miss , orchestrator .

questions.q: The data team says: "We discovered a lineage gap - we cannot trace where this field originated." What is data lineage ?
options: Historical data stored in a slowly changing dimension.
The network graph of database foreign key relationships.
A compliance term for how long data must be retained.
The traceable path of a data field through systems - from its origin (source system) through all transformations to its final form in reports.
questions.explanation: Data lineage = "where did this number come from?" It answers the question of how data has flowed and been transformed from source to report. Lineage use case Benefit Impact analysis If a source column changes, which downstream models break? Data quality debugging Trace anomalies back to the root cause transformation Compliance (GDPR) Prove data provenance and demonstrate audit trail Tools: OpenLineage, Atlan, DataHub, dbt lineage graph. Key vocabulary: data provenance , lineage graph , impact analysis , upstream source dependency .

questions.q: A data engineer says: "The SLA requires the reporting dataset to be fresh by 6am." What does "data freshness" mean in a pipeline context?
options: The data was ingested from a real-time source rather than batch files.
The data uses current column naming conventions.
The data is sufficiently up-to-date - it was last updated within the expected freshness window.
The data has passed data quality validation checks.
questions.explanation: Data freshness SLO = the maximum allowed lag before data is considered stale. Concept Definition Freshness check Compare max(updated_at) vs. current time Freshness SLO e.g., data must be no older than 2 hours Staleness Data has exceeded the freshness threshold Tools: dbt source freshness , Great Expectations freshness check. Key vocabulary: freshness SLO , staleness , freshness alert , data availability SLA , pipeline latency .

questions.q: PR Description Subject: Update to User Profile Data Pipeline - Added Delta Lake Support Hi Team, Please review. We've integrated Delta Lake for improved data consistency and rollback capabilities within the user profile data pipeline. This allows us to efficiently handle schema changes without disrupting downstream consumers. Thanks, John
options: Delta Lake primarily focuses on optimizing batch processing jobs within the pipeline, not evolving schemas.
Implementing Delta Lake means we've reduced our reliance on external database systems for storing user profile data.
Delta Lake provides a mechanism for managing large datasets by partitioning them into smaller, more manageable pieces, improving query performance.
The PR demonstrates the implementation of a new data transformation stage using Delta Lake to ensure schema evolution is handled atomically and consistently.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of a common PR description related to Delta Lake integration. The correct answer highlights that Delta Lake is used for atomic schema evolution - crucial when dealing with changing data structures in pipelines. Options C and D misrepresent Delta Lake's core function; it's not about partitioning or reducing reliance on databases, but rather about managing schema changes *within* the pipeline itself. Option A is incorrect as Delta Lake focuses heavily on transactional capabilities and consistency.

questions.q: During a code review of the new user profile pipeline PR, Sarah asks: 'Why did we switch to using Change Data Capture (CDC) instead of polling the CRM database? The previous approach was simpler.' What is the primary advantage of CDC over periodic polling in this scenario?
options: Polling is generally cheaper to implement initially due to its simpler architecture compared to a CDC system.
CDC offers better fault tolerance; if the CRM database becomes unavailable, polling will automatically retry indefinitely.
Polling provides a more granular view of data changes , allowing for near real-time updates and reducing latency.
CDC minimizes load on the CRM database by only capturing new records as they are created, rather than repeatedly querying the entire dataset.
questions.explanation: The core benefit of Change Data Capture (CDC) lies in its efficiency and reduced impact on source systems. Polling involves repeatedly querying a database - this creates significant load, especially with large datasets. CDC, conversely, only captures *new* data changes as they occur, minimizing the strain on the CRM database and significantly improving performance; Sarah's concern about simplicity is misleading because CDC offers more robust and scalable change management.

questions.q: Mark is explaining a new data pipeline to the team. He says, "We're using Kafka Streams for real-time processing of clickstream events." What does 'Kafka Streams' primarily refer to in this context?
options: A: A fully managed database service optimized for low-latency queries.
B: A stream processing library within the Apache Kafka ecosystem that allows you to build real-time applications.
C: A message queue designed specifically for handling large volumes of data with guaranteed delivery.
D: An API endpoint for accessing clickstream event data from a third-party vendor.
questions.explanation: Kafka Streams is a powerful stream processing library built *on top* of Kafka. It allows developers to write applications that consume and transform streams of data in real-time, making it ideal for scenarios like clickstream analysis where immediate insights are needed. Options A, C, and D describe other related technologies or services; Kafka Streams specifically focuses on the *processing* aspect.

questions.q: Sarah comments in a code review: 'This pipeline uses a nightly batch job to load data from our legacy system. It's inefficient and introduces latency.' What is the most likely issue Sarah is highlighting regarding this approach?
options: A: The use of a relational database for storing large datasets.
B: The lack of real-time processing capabilities, resulting in delayed data updates.
C: The reliance on a centralized data warehouse for all reporting needs.
D: The implementation of complex ETL transformations within the pipeline.
questions.explanation: Sarah's comment points to the inefficiency of batch loading. Nightly batch jobs are inherently slow and create latency because they process data in large chunks at scheduled intervals. This contrasts with approaches that allow for more immediate updates or real-time processing. Options A, C, and D represent different technical aspects that aren't directly causing the problem described.

questions.q: A Kafka architect explains: "The topic has 12 partitions with a replication factor of 3." What does a replication factor of 3 mean?
options: Three different Kafka clusters are synchronised.
Each partition has 3 copies across different broker nodes - 1 leader and 2 followers - providing fault tolerance if up to 2 brokers fail.
The topic retains data for 3 days before expiry.
Each message is processed by 3 different consumers.
questions.explanation: Replication factor = number of broker copies of each partition: Role Function Leader Handles all reads and writes for the partition Followers Replicate leader data; promote on leader failure Minimum recommended: RF=3 for production. RF=3 tolerates up to 2 broker failures. Key vocabulary: leader partition , follower replication , ISR (In-Sync Replicas) , unclean leader election , acks=all for durability .

questions.q: A team has two consumer instances in the same consumer group reading from a 6-partition topic. How are partitions assigned?
options: Kafka randomly assigns partitions per message.
One consumer reads all partitions; the second is a standby.
Each consumer reads from half the partitions (3 each) - Kafka rebalances partitions across consumers in the group.
Both consumers read all 6 partitions simultaneously, deduplicating messages.
questions.explanation: Consumer group = cooperative partition consumption - each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer in the group: Scenario Assignment 6 partitions, 2 consumers 3 partitions each 6 partitions, 6 consumers 1 partition each (max parallelism) 6 partitions, 8 consumers 2 consumers sit idle Key vocabulary: consumer group rebalance , partition assignment , lag monitoring , committed offset , at-least-once vs. exactly-once .

questions.q: A monitoring alert fires: "The consumer group is at 45,000 messages lag on partition 3." What does consumer lag indicate?
options: The partition has 45,000 messages that have expired and been deleted.
The consumer has not yet processed 45,000 messages that have been produced - it is behind the producer.
The consumer is processing messages 45,000ms slower than expected.
There are 45,000 messages that have been read but not yet acknowledged.
questions.explanation: Consumer lag = latest_offset − committed_offset Lag situation Likely cause Sudden large lag spike Consumer crash, temporary partition reassignment Slowly growing lag Consumer throughput below producer rate Stable lag Consumer keeping pace but behind (acceptable in some systems) Key vocabulary: consumer lag , offset commit , lag monitoring (Kafka UI, Burrow) , backpressure , lag recovery rate .

questions.q: An engineer explains: "The streaming pipeline uses event-time windowing rather than processing-time windowing." What is the key difference?
options: Event-time orders and windows events by when they actually occurred (the event's own timestamp) - correctly handling out-of-order and late-arriving events; processing-time windows by when the system received the event.
Event-time uses the Kafka timestamp; processing-time uses wall-clock time.
Event-time windowing is only available in Apache Flink.
Processing-time provides stricter exactly-once semantics.
questions.explanation: Event-time vs. processing-time windowing : Time domain Based on Challenge Event-time Timestamp embedded in the event payload Late/out-of-order events require watermarks Processing-time Wall-clock time when event arrives at processor Inaccurate for events delayed in transit Key vocabulary: watermark , late data handling , allowed lateness , window trigger , tumbling vs. sliding vs. session window .

questions.q: A system design document states: "The pipeline guarantees exactly-once delivery semantics." What does exactly-once semantics mean and why is it hard to achieve?
options: Each message is processed precisely once - no duplicates and no data loss - even across failures requiring retries.
Each message is processed at least once and duplicates can be filtered downstream.
Messages are delivered in the exact order they were produced.
Each message is processed at most once - some messages may be lost but none are duplicated.
questions.explanation: Delivery guarantees - the fundamental trade-off in distributed messaging: Guarantee Trade-off Implementation At-most-once May lose messages, no duplicates Fire and forget At-least-once No loss, may duplicate Retry on failure Exactly-once No loss, no duplicates (hardest) Idempotent producer + transactional API Key vocabulary: idempotent producer , transactional API , 2PC in streaming , semantic guarantee trade-offs , Flink checkpointing .

questions.q: Sarah : 'Okay team, I've deployed the new Kafka consumer. We're seeing a lot of errors related to out-of-order messages in our analytics dashboard. The logs show that some consumers are receiving messages before others, despite running on the same cluster and consuming from the same topic.' Which of the following best explains Sarah 's observation regarding message order in Kafka?
options: Kafka's inherent distributed nature means messages can be processed out of order due to the asynchronous nature of its commit process; this requires careful design for ordered processing.
The Kafka brokers are experiencing network latency, causing messages to arrive out of sequence. This is a standard Kafka behavior that needs to be tolerated.
The consumer group configuration isn't correctly set up, leading to consumers attempting to read from the same partition simultaneously without proper synchronization.
The topic itself is configured with an invalid replication factor, causing brokers to deliver messages in a non-deterministic order.
questions.explanation: Sarah 's observation points to a fundamental characteristic of Kafka's distributed architecture. Because Kafka brokers replicate data across multiple nodes asynchronously, there's no guarantee that all consumers will receive the same message at exactly the same time. This inherent delay and asynchronous commit process can result in messages being processed out of order; it is not a bug but rather a consequence of how Kafka handles fault tolerance and scalability. Option B describes a symptom, not the root cause. Options C and D are incorrect because they attribute the issue to consumer configuration or topic settings respectively - while these *can* contribute to ordering issues, they aren't the primary driver.

questions.q: David : 'Hey team, I've just updated the Kafka producer to use a higher batch size. We should see an improvement in throughput!' Maria : 'I'm seeing some increased latency on our dashboards since the update. The consumer group is struggling to keep up with the incoming data volume.' Which of the following best describes the potential root cause of Maria's observation, given David's change?
options: The increased batch size has negatively impacted message ordering within the Kafka topic, leading to consumer delays due to needing to re-sequence messages.
The increased batch size automatically optimized the consumer group's processing rate, eliminating any potential latency issues.
David's change directly caused a failure in the Kafka cluster, requiring immediate intervention from operations.
A decrease in the number of partitions allocated to the topic has resulted in increased competition among consumers and higher latency.
questions.explanation: Incorrect options often assume direct causation or focus on unrelated problems. The core issue here is related to Kafka's producer-consumer model and how batching affects message ordering. A larger batch size from the producer increases the likelihood of messages being processed in a non-sequential order by consumers, as they are grouped together before delivery. This creates contention for the consumer group, causing latency as consumers must resequence messages - not a failure of the cluster or a reduction in partitions.

options: The Kafka producer is sending messages with invalid serialization formats, resulting in errors during consumption.
